utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a procedural matter left over from yesterday concerning transcripts of -- Mr. Cayley can deal with, which might just clear the decks on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you will recall with the witness Mr. Skegro that on re-examination he was shown two documents, one was the HINA report and one was the Helsinki Committee report. And you had asked, I think specifically you said so that the Appeals Chamber can see that we were completely transparent about these matters, that they'd be uploaded into e-court and they have. And just for the purposes of the transcript, the Helsinki Committee report is now uploaded as 2D17-4497, and the HINA report as 2D17-4482.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. They both were in English from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now usually we would not accept anything into evidence unless it would be translated into the language of the accused as well. Under the present circumstances I'm addressing the parties whether there would be any problem in admitting them, although they would only be available in one of the official languages of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, Mr. President, I think the HINA report was in Croatian, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- was it in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was read into the transcript, Your Honour, will recollect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I understood what it said. Well, then I think for the Appeals Chamber not being certain about their proficiency in B/C/S, perhaps, Mr. Cayley, we could finalise the matter once the HINA report is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is only six or seven lines, I think. So it's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, so it is just the extract. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then we will ask Mr. Registrar to -- would we make them one exhibit or two separate exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think two separate exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two separate exhibits. Then, Mr. Registrar, the -- the Helsinki Committee report 2D17-4497 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would become Exhibit D1685.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and may I take it that there are no objections against admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carrier. D1685 is admitted into evidence. The HINA report, Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number for it to be MFI'd and once a translation is there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's 65 ter 2D17-4482, and that becomes Exhibit D1686.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, keeps the status of MFI for the time being. May I take it that once there is a translation uploaded that there will be no objections against admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carrier. Then apart from this, Mr. Kay, are further procedural matters, or are we ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are no more. May the witness be called. Mr. Lukovic, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration before you give testimony. The text will now be handed out to you by the Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I read this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, is it correct that you gave a statement in the year 2004 to the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the document 2D00-708 could be put on the screen before the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukovic, you will see two screens in front of you. The right-hand screen will shortly show you a document, and I'd like you to have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The signatures, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There we have the last page of the document that was a record of your interview with the Office of the Prosecution. Is that your signature at the end of that document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see my signature in the page that is shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the English also shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the next page of the one, page 11. Maybe that will help. We've gone to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we go to page 11, where there is, in the English language, a witness acknowledgment. Is that your signature there on the witness acknowledgment?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now turn to another document, 2D00-709.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the document on the right-hand side, this is in the Croatian language, and if you could look at your signature at the bottom of the first page, do you recognise that as your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we could just go to the last of those pages for that document, page 15, please, in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise there your signature with the date on the left-hand side, of the 13th of August, 2009?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this statement which you gave to the Defence, is it correct that you made a number of corrections to the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecution in the year 2004?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, taking into account the information that you gave in your statement to the Office of the Prosecution and the corrections that you made to that statement in the statement to the Defence and the information contained in that second statement, is the totality of those statements, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The last statement and the changes it contains are the truth, to the best of my knowledge and recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the first statement, putting to one side the matters that you disagreed with in that statement to the Office of the Prosecution which you later corrected, is the rest of the information in that statement, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And taking into account, then, the information in both of those two statements that you have directed as being correct, if I were to ask you the same questions in court today, would you give the same answers as you previously gave in those statements that are correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I would give you the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, I move that both of those documents be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, first the 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 2D00-708 becomes Exhibit D1687.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the next document is 65 ter 2D00-709. That becomes Exhibit D1688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is also admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. Contained within those two statements are also documents which I move should become exhibits. First of all, 2D00-169, which is referred to in paragraph 6 of the Defence statement of 2009. I move that that goes into evidence as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may be aware that the numbers always -- that is the -- paragraph 6, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: OBR06 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would refer to the content approximately then I know exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 6 of the statement, Your Honour. It's basic instructions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- for the work of the UN and EU liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the one which was already in -- on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Carrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you also express already on the two other documents whether there is any objection against having it added to the 65 ter list, that is, the radio silence letter dated the 4th of August; and the -- could I say the Kenyan soldiers letter also of the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection to either of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, Mr. Kay, the leave is granted to add them to the 65 ter list as was requested in your motion. And then I expect that you would tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. And the document, then, 2D00-710 which is referred to in the OTP statement at paragraph 20, I ask that that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from Mr. Carrier or from any of the other Defence teams. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I show we have two documents currently tendered. The first is 65 ter 2D00-169. That becomes Exhibit D1689. The second document is 65 ter number 2D00-710, and that becomes Exhibit D1690.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are -- both are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is 2D00-711, referred to in paragraph 21 of the OTP statement. I request that that be put into evidence as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections against that. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll give a very brief statement now of the summary of the contents of those two statements, and then I have a few questions to ask Mr. Lukovic concerning some other documents to be tendered and also ready in the case. Mr. Lukovic was the chief of the Department for Cooperation with the UN and EC of the Croatian Army for Sector South. In 1995, he went to Knin on the 5th of August, and he met General Cermak there on the 6th of August. Mr. Lukovic describes the nature of his work as a liaison officer liaising between the international community and the Croatian military, describing that his tasks took him sometimes from a military role to also dealing with civilian issues. He describes the nature of Mr. Cermak's work in Knin, in that he assisted the civilian authorities to establish the conditions for normal life as soon as possible and to restore the town and return it to a functional state as soon as possible. Initially all the installations from power stations, telephone stations, water supply, and other services were disabled, he believes, by the Serbs before they left. Along with solving the problems of the town in Knin, Mr. Cermak also made contact with the United Nations representatives on a daily basis, and he attempted to help the refugees who were located at the UN camp in Knin. Mr. Lukovic was also, likewise, engaged on similar work with Mr. Cermak. And he describes the fact that Mr. Cermak was not in command of either the military police or the civilian police, and from his knowledge, when crimes were informed to Mr. Cermak by the international community, he passed on the details that had been given to him to the civilian police or the military police. Your Honour, that ends the brief summary of the statements. There are now some documents I would like the witness to look at. The first matter is an exhibit, D318, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, I'd like you to look at a document on the screen. We will, first of all, look at the first page. It's a document dated the 6th of August, 1995, and it's signed by Brigadier Plestina, whom you describe in your statement as being your immediate superior in your department. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document we're looking at are the minutes of a meeting with a Colonel Pettis who was chief of the UNCRO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we just turn to page 2 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukovic, it's correct, is it not, that you can read both languages; you can read English as well as being a native Croatian speaker?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't say that I'm fully bilingual but to quite a large extent, I can read both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I suspect most of us here will be looking at the English document, although I may have got that wrong in this case. If we look at this first page here, you can see that it's a description of a meeting between Brigadier Plestina and Colonel Pettis. First of all, have you seen these minutes from this meeting before?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the form of minutes. But Brigadier Plestina briefed me about the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of the documents -- of the document, he refers to liaison officers contacting him by the UN phone in -- in Knin. Is that a matter that you know about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed about it. Brigadier Plestina drew my attention to it; Brigadier Plestina was my superior. He told me that it was a fortunate thing that Colonel Pettis, the Chief of Staff, who told him that the Croatian Army had not gotten in contact with the military representatives in Knin to which Brigadier Plestina responded that I was the one who had contacted him by phone in the UN headquarters in Knin, and that was a fortunate thing. I believe that the office from which I called was Colonel Blahna's office, and he was the Deputy Commander of UN in Knin. So when I arrived at the UN headquarters in Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's all the detail we'll need on that. I just wanted you to confirm that fact from you. In relation to the next paragraph, if you could just read that paragraph to yourself, and -- before you answer some questions.

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You will see that this paragraph refers to a discussion between Colonel Pettis and Brigadier Plestina concerning freedom of movement. And Brigadier Plestina here refers to the fact that he refused a request from Colonel Pettis concerning freedom of movement, and he gave the reason about the battle has still been carrying on. In relation to this matter discussed between the two men on the 6th of August, were you aware of the request being made to Brigadier Plestina to give freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Knin at that time, and the phone lines were down, so that I did not learn of this promptly or in a short period of time, but I learned of it later on. But how much later on, I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can move on to another document now, which is 2D00-319.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 7th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court may remember there was an extract of this document dealing with Sector South, which is the one that we've had uploaded in the court. D319. Can I call up D319? I've got a different document here for D319. That looks to me like something else entirely. There. That I do recognise. Can we go to page 3 of the Croatian document, leaving the English document on the page, as it is an extract, as the Court will remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you see at the bottom of this page here in the Croatian language that the paragraph concerns liberated territory of the former Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of the Croatian, again leaving the English document as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is another daily report from Brigadier Plestina, Mr. Lukovic, and you can see in the paragraph at the top of the page that it refers to: "The office of our UNCRO liaison officer has been established." Would that be your office?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my office in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go through that paragraph further, if you could just read it to yourself. You'll see in the first meeting with General Forand they mainly talked about unfounded complaints that UNCRO filed in Knin, they were primarily Canadians, regarding the restriction of movement. Then it says: "Our liaison officer explained to General Forand that UNCRO has complete freedom of movement regarding the supply of the units on the field but there is no need for their patrols, observations from their observation points, and reports on breaching of Zagreb Agreement, since the situation at the moment is such that the higher authorities will decide on the potential new UNCRO task?" Firstly, does this paragraph refer to a meeting that you had with General Forand?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the first meetings I had with General Forand, and we discussed this matter, and this is exactly the position that I took. In other words, I explained that the situation had completely changed in the field and that the various tenets of various UN Resolutions that were in force before Operation Storm simply were no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware on the occasion of the 7th of August of the existence of an agreement between Mr. Akashi, on behalf of the UN, and Mr. Sarinic, on behalf of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned of that agreement. However, I cannot claim with certainty when it was that I learned of it exactly, but certainly not shortly after it, because the phone lines and the fax lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now turn to another document, D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this same document of the 7th we find that a visit by General Janvier to Knin were -- was approved by Mr. Sarinic. Now, you said, We -- the phone lines were down so we couldn't learn about the agreement concluded between Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi. Here, in this document, I find, at least an indication that -- a decision of Mr. Sarinic, that you were aware of that, which suggests that, at least, there was some communication, despite the fact that the phone lines were down, as you said. Could you -- could you comment on what this letter does suggest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will gladly reply. The source of information that I had, information on any new positions or instructions from Zagreb, was -- or came to me through various means. Either I would go to Sibenik to make a phone call, or someone would come to Knin from Zagreb and relay the information, or some similar method. I told you that I did learn of this agreement, but I cannot say with certainty when exactly, on what date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just assist, maybe this would help, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this remark here concerning Mr. Sarinic, is it right that this is not your report; this is Mr. Plestina's report, Brigadier Plestina's report?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The report that we see in front of us, I would appreciate it if you could understand one thing. I was the chief officer for Sector South. And on those days, when the phone lines were still down in Knin, as well as the fax lines, the lines with Zagreb, the reports for Sector South where we were liaison officers were sent by my deputy, Colonel Dragic, from our seat in Zadar. Therefore, you see this information for these other places that are mentioned there, Rasovic and so on, can you see it in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I may have been, to some extent imprecise, but the letter shows more examples of apparently the reporting person knows what happens on the grounds in Knin and apparently, if we're talking about a visit to Knin, and if it is approved I would expect Knin to know about that, and it was scheduled apparently for the day after the 7th. So, therefore, I was just wondering about what communication was there, because the mere fact that telephone lines were not functioning, apparently did not disturb all sorts of communication. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Next document I'd like to us look at is 2D00-10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 9th of August, 1995, from the chief of the Croatian Army Main Staff, General Cervenko. And it's headed: "In order to enable the normal security of the movement of ... UNCRO forces," he orders: "1. Secure unobstructed deployment of the UNCRO units according to the schedule existing before Operation Storm began as well as the unobstructed supplying." Firstly, is this a document that you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see this document at the time, although we did discuss it indirectly. In other words, I kept in touch with some individuals - I can't recall exactly who - who was aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matter that this concerns in -- in point 1, are you able to assist the Court as to what this issue concerned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, UNCRO units in Sector South were deployed at the level -- at the battalion level. A battalion consisted of three subordinate units, companies, so these UN battalions did not -- did not go into action together. They were dispersed throughout the territory. They were in smaller groups, deployed in smaller groups in certain observation posts and so forth. The entire deployment of these various UN units and elements, even before Operation Storm -- or, rather, from the very beginning, when they arrived in this area, so we were aware through our cooperation with the UN of their deployments which was a necessity in wartime, in order to avoid some harm to come to those UN units. So, I am rather certain, and I can even claim, that after Operation Storm, because all these small groups were in the field, the intention of UN commanders was to group these units in one area, at the company level or the battalion level. And I believe that this is what this order refers to. The reason I know this is because my subordinate communication officers provided reports from various areas in the former Sector South where they actually assisted these commanders in gathering and collecting these various elements in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this document. Might this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1692.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1692 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is 2D00-386. It's a document dated the 13th of August, 1995, from General Cervenko again. And it's headed: "As per the new military and political situation after Operation Storm and with regard to the announcement of the UNCRO command on re-deployment of their units." And we can see in the body of the order that, from the 16th of August, unobstructed departure of UNCRO forces with equipment and devices was to take place. And we can see at the bottom left-hand corner that this was sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, office for the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, just to establish this, is this a document that you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see this document either, personally, but I was indirectly aware of it, informed of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the issue this concerns about the unobstructed departure of UNCRO forces, are you able to assist the Court as to what this issue was about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the foundation for this document is similar to the earlier document that I explained. This had to do with new developments with the collection of these various units in one location so that then, under a new command, they would be able to move from that point elsewhere more easily. But, as I said, this is closely related to the previous question that you mentioned -- that you asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've no further questions, Your Honour, I move that this document be admitted into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1693 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And now the last document that I need to look at is 2D00-428.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a letter dated the 26th of August, 1995, from Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes, sent to the Croatian Army office for the UN and ECMM for Sector South, Zadar. It's headed: "Restriction of Movement." And states: "Respected Navy Captain." And then refers, in paragraph 1 -- if could you look at that document, Mr. Lukovic, to a UNMO patrol from Sibenik being stopped at a police check-point. And it was stated that if the UNMO patrol approached this check-point again they'd be shot. "This patrol was made to carry out a humanitarian mission." Paragraph 3 refers to the fact that this was a denial of access in direct contravention of the Zagreb Agreement of the 6th of August and of General Cermak's letter dated 11th August, 1995. And it says: "I will ask to you to address this letter to the right authorities for a positive solution." Firstly, was this letter addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it was addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the matter raised in this letter, do you have any comments to make upon that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I do. This was on the 26th of August, and, at this time, the military observers and generally military personnel had no difficulty moving along the Knin-Zadar-Sibenik communication lines. However, again we see that this has to do with some sort of patrol. Now let me just explain to you very briefly that throughout the war, A, all patrols by UNMOs had to be announced to my office and then our liaison officer would join these patrols and -- and accompany them on their beat. So I cannot tell you exactly what patrol this was about, but, A, it probably was unannounced; and, 2, it was stopped by the civilian police which is something that I cannot really comment on, because as we look at the date mentioned there, this is already the time when the civilian police authorities were already in place. And I don't know what type of patrols the military observers would be on, regardless of what they referred to it as, whether it was humanitarian patrol or whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions on that matter. And, Your Honour, that concludes my questions of -- of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm rightly reminded to exhibit this document, if I may, with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was waiting for that. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1694.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1694 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Wait there, please, Mr. Lukovic. There will be some more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Lukovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Carrier. Mr. Carrier is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, during your first meeting with General Cermak on the 7th of August, 1995, I take it he did not fully explain to you his precise role in Knin. I think you said in your statement that he told he was there to assist with normalization. Moreover, in your 2004 statement, that's the one you gave to the Prosecution, you said that you weren't personally aware of or didn't know why such a high-ranking officer had been assigned to the Knin garrison position. Mr. Lukovic, my question to you is: Did you ever learn the details of who had appointed General Cermak or what specifically he was tasked with doing in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: My level, the level of my duties and my rank, was not authorised or did not have clearance to learn such information. The only information that I did learn was at meetings at the Knin fortress. And what I could see there throughout my stay in Knin and what -- and that's what I could see of what General Cermak did and what his tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukovic, is it fair to say, then, that do you not know the precise parameters of the authority that was granted to General Cermak for his role in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking whether I ever saw a document on the appointment of General Cermak, my answer is no, I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's good enough. Mr. Lukovic, did you follow the testimony of Mr. Franjo Feldi who was called to testify last week in this case as an expert for General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was on the island, and I did not have technical capabilities that would allow me to follow that testimony. So, to answer your question, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Did anyone in any way inform you about anything that Mr. Feldi said during his testimony last week?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I know that he testified. I know that Mr. Skegro testified. I saw that on TV. And I know that Mr. Rincic testified as well. But I don't know any details of their testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, are you able to explain the circumstances of a meeting that took place between you and Mr. Plestina and Mr. Feldi in the Central Military Archives approximately three years ago?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Feldi last -- approximately three years ago. We were invited to come to the archives. Somebody wanted to write a book or papers or something of the kind about the war in Croatia and about Storm. We met for the first time and General Feldi was there, but I was never invited, and I never went there after that initial meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, who exactly invited you to the archives?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was General Lovric, from the Main Staff. But I'm not sure. I believe that it was either him or somebody, a staff member, from his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember if Mr. Pokaz was there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not at that initial meeting. I don't think that Mr. Pokaz was there the moment when I saw Mr. Feldi. But I believe that I came across him either on that day or around that time. But I repeat, he was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Rakic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Rakic certainly did not attend that meeting, although he had been invited to Zagreb on account of the same matter. And since Mr. Rakic and I are neighbours, I know that he went to Zagreb on a similar business. He told me that himself. However, I don't know how long he stayed or how many times he went to Zagreb on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You say that you had this initial meeting in the archives and then you never went back. Did you have subsequent meetings, though, with General Lovric and General Pokaz and General Feldi about writing this book, that you call it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the book, because I learned that subsequently from a third person, not from any of the persons that you just mentioned. And initially when I arrived there, I agreed that I would author one part of that book. Because it had been announced to me that the material would be used in defence of our Generals. Later on, I learned that the project would be a book, and I withdrew from that project. So I don't know how things evolved after that. I apologise, you asked me about General Lovric. I did meet with General Lovric after that, only once, and on that occasion, I informed -- informed him that I wouldn't -- no longer wished to participate in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just to clarify something: Did you actually write a part of the book with Mr. Plestina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No way can you -- anybody say that I authored a part of that book. I did write a few pages of the text during the period when we still thought that the material would be used in defence of our Generals present here in this courtroom. Later on, when I learned that the materials would probably be used for a book, I went to see General Lovric, and I withdrew from the project. In other words, I did not author a single sentence for that book, or in that book. I don't know if I have made myself clear enough, or do you perhaps seek further clarification from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, I don't have any more questions on that point. Mr. Lukovic, in your statements you discuss the reporting system for your department and the CALOs, I'll call them CALOs. Those are Croatian Army liaison officers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what period you are referring to. Are you asking me in general how the system functioned during the homeland war, or are you referring to the couple of days or maybe three days in Knin before telephone and other communication lines were established?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is August 1995. But I'll take you through some things first, and if there's things you want to clear up after, you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call up document number 2D00-169, which is actually now Exhibit - I apologise - D1689.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, what's coming up on the screen is what you've described as the basic instructions. And if I could direct your attention to number 3 -- item number 3 on page 1 in the English, which is also page 1 in B/C/S, where - and correct me if I'm wrong - where CALO reporting is discussed. I'll just read it to you, and it says: "The liaison officers of the Ministry of Defence department office for UN and EU are obligated to report in writing and by telephone to this office directly or via the head of their department, as well as the authorised commander of the OZ (HRM) every day and regularly of their activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It continues: "The report needs to contain clearly marked activity of the officer (of the Department), situation on the relevant area, assessment, evaluation of the development of the action and proposal for procedure." Now, Mr. Lukovic, reading that, is it that the basic instructions require the CALOs to report to the HV Military District Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The reports were not sent to the HV Military District Command. The activities that needed to be carried out were agreed directly with the commander or another person from the command. As for the daily reports, they were sent to Brigadier Plestina's office, which was in Zagreb in a written form. When it comes to the reporting on other re -- events, if necessary, those reports were sent to the HV Military District Commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, is it just that the written reports, not written, but they are required, pursuant to item 3 in the basic instructions, to inform the Military District Command every day and regularly of their activities; just that it doesn't have to be in a written form?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much you understand the role of CALOs. We were a link between the commands and commanders of the Croatian Army at different levels where CALOs were positioned, and the commands and commanders of the UN on the other hand. Their mutual agreements, their joint activities of any kind, were discussed through the office for liaison of the Croatian Army. Of course, if the commander of a Military District needed to meet with, for example, the UN commander for Sector South, then we would send such an invitation from our office, and when we received an answer from the UN command, we obviously reported back to the Military District Commander who requested such a meeting and vice versa. What other reports do you think we should have sent? What other needs do you think for reporting were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, it's -- just to be clear. What I'm trying to understand is your boss's understanding of what CALOs are supposed to do. Major Plestina who signed this basic instruction, and he's the one that in item 3 says that they're supposed to basically report. And it says that they're supposed to do that to the authorised commander of the OZ everyday and regularly, other activities, and it goes on to detail what the reports require. So that's what I'm interested in, not the role -- not the role of CALOs. I'm interested in that and whether or not that was happening during August 1995, whether or not that report was happening.

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The situation that concerned daily reporting to the commander of the OZ or somebody from the Command Staff did happen every day until August 1995. Because the UN patrols, i.e., the military observers' patrols went to the areas where Croatian troops were deployed. And obviously they had to be announced every time they wanted to go there, and obviously the command had and needed to know about that. Most probably it would be the commander himself. And after such patrols, if there had been some objections on the part of the UN, the Military District would receive feedback. And you can call those feedbacks reports. Maybe this is what you're talking about, when the Military Districts and the HV troops are concerned. In paragraph number 3, Mr. Plestina does not elaborate on that, because we're talking about the first day of the existence of this department for UN. And his further practice showed that he insisted on daily reports once a day or several times a day, if needed, to be sent to Zagreb. As for the activities of the military observers and liaison officers on the ground could not go unobserved or without the commander or the command of the Military District unnotified, or if those patrols took place at a lower level, then it would be lower level commands that had to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just trying to understand something you said. You said that that kind of reporting I described before was happening up until August 1995. And then you describe what was, presumably, what was happening during August 1995. Please correct me if I'm wrong, but my question relates to that, which is, are you able to explain why in your statement you said that you were meeting regularly, yourself with General Gotovina, and you said four or five times a week, after he was appointed to the Split Military District Command Post, and yet you state that you had no contact with General Gotovina after the 6th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: My contacts with General Gotovina as the HV Military District Commander depended on either his request for activities or information that would be provided to the UN or the European Community Mission, or vice versa, if a request came from the UN towards the authorised command of the Croatian Army in the territory. In other words, throughout all the time from the moment General Gotovina was appointed the commander of the OZ, which later became a Military District, the developments and activities of the UN on the ground and whatever concerned representatives of the international community were so intense that most commonly, as I've already told you, this happened five days a week. And I'd adhere by my words. Which means that I did not contact him personally, although there were often personal contacts with him, but with his deputy or a member of his staff, if the other two were otherwise engaged. The intensity of developments on the ground and the need for communication between the representatives of the Croatian Army and the representatives of the UN was such that such frequent meetings were indeed necessary. If you want, and I apologise, there were daily patrols, UN patrols, at least in four or five different directions, and the commanded needed to be informed of those patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So if I can understand this, you're saying that if you were requested by the Split Military District Command to come and talk to them, you would; and if the situation on the ground became so intense that, given, presumably, that the Split Military District Command, who was in charge of the area, you would then take it upon yourself to go to the Split Military District Command and tell them what was happening and what information you had from internationals, given the intensity of the situation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid I didn't understand the question. Some of the elements in the question are really unclear to me. What do you mean when you say me going to Split personally? Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, a question of a less composite character might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Lukovic. Number one, if you or your department, or the CALOs, so anyone in your department or under your control, if the Split Military District Command wanted to talk to you, they could basically summon you; right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, alternatively, you or the CALOs or your department, if the situation on the ground reached an intensity that required -- or you felt that required informing the area commander, that you would then take it upon yourself to go and -- and tell them what was happening?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe since you're asking me that that what you have in mind the role of a CALO, and what does it mean when you are asking me about war, when the situation is intense, how can I see something that nobody else sees? Why are you asking me that? We're talking about a war situation. I don't know what it is that I could have noticed that required me to go and inform the HV Military District Commander, me being a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, maybe it'll help if you just read you your words and can you explain it to me. Beginning around page 29, just for reference purposes, saying: "... although there were often personal contacts with him," -- meaning General Gotovina, "but with his deputy or a member of his staff, if the other two were otherwise engaged. "The intensity of developments on the ground and need for communication between representative of the Croatian Army and the representatives of the UN was such that such frequent meetings were indeed necessary." So that was what I was referring to when I was asking you about the intensity of the situation on the ground. I was wondering if you could explain that. And my question was: If the situation on the ground reached a level of intensity that basically required that you would have to then go and tell the HV commanders what is was happening; that was the question.

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if your question is related to what you've just quoted, I repeat, my office, my department, maintained a dual connection. One side of that coin was when the HV Military District called me and asked me to do things for them, for him; and the second facet of that was, for example, a request would reach me from the side of the UN requesting a meeting with our commander or a member of a Command Staff. In that case, we would receive a written request to that effect. We would then translate it, and then either me or my deputy would take that paper to the command -- to the commander personally or to his secretary or to a staff member there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, correct me if I'm wrong, but is what you're describing in terms of your role, and the role of your department, is simply to go back and forth between the HV and the UN but not to make any kind of independent assessment about any information that's coming to you in terms of informing anybody about what you're learning from either side?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to CALOs' activities, and we were CALOs - and that term is coined of two words, the first one is "officer" and the second one is "liaison." As an officer of the Croatian Army, whenever I came across a thing on the ground, a phenomenon on ground, before or after the month of August 1995 not just me but all the other officers had to react and try and assist with any situation which we might have encountered on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So if you were being informed constantly about crimes being committed on the ground, given what you just described as the role, would you have then taken upon yourself to go and inform the Military District Commander, or the command, about what was happening in their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: In all of my reports, before Operation Storm, you -- we could not testify about any crimes on the ground. As for what we saw in the situation that we found ourselves in after Operation Storm, there were situations when we came across such things and then we informed about that. Most commonly we would inform the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just to go back briefly to what you were say about CALOs. And you said the second letter stands for "army." Why would you be going to tell the civilian police, given that you're a member of the army, your role is to liaise between the army and internationals? Can you explain that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period after Operation Storm, then I can tell you that I personally adhered to one thing, and I still adhere to that, and stand by that. On the third day after Operation Storm, I heard over the public media that -- I heard a piece of news that the previously occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia were reintegrated back into the -- integrated back into the system the constitutional and legal system of Croatia. So, for me, on the fourth day after Operation Storm, or today, if I compare the two situations, there is no difference. If I were to be a witness to a crime, any type of criminal activity, I would only then go to the civilian police to report that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll come back to this, but if I could -- perhaps now is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the right time for a break. We will have a break, and we will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I would be inclined to invite to you continue, but without a witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, just to start where we left off and just to refresh your memory a little bit. You said that after Operation Storm you heard through the public media -- you heard a piece of news that the former occupied territories had been reintegrated into -- into the Croatian legal system. And you said that that was on the fourth day after Storm or so. What day is that, if you can recall, like, the actual date?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what date it was, but I think it was on the third day following Operation Storm, not on the fourth day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And is it that -- because of what you heard on the news, you then started to report crimes or whatever you heard about happening, you started reporting that to the civilian police because of the news item that you heard?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes; but not solely for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could explore that. Because -- correct me if I'm wrong, but you don't take orders as a member of the army from media broadcasts. So was there an order to that effect, that you were supposed to stop reporting, however you were before, and start reporting to the civilian police about any crime you see?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no orders to that effect, other than a visit that I received in Knin from my superior, Brigadier Plestina, and we discussed these matters as well, on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Is that before or after you heard the news item that, in your mind, changed where you had to report crimes to? Sorry, just to be clear, the visit from Mr. Plestina.

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. First, I heard the report in the news media; and then, after that, Brigadier Plestina came to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So in the interim, between the news broadcast and the visit from Mr. Plestina, you were -- you stopped reporting to people in the army, and you started reporting to the civilian police about crimes you were becoming aware of?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. There may be an interpretation error. But it is not about reporting on crimes. Rather, if you noticed or observed anything happening in the field or were informed by someone, in that case, we would brief on that. That's number one. Number two, in those day, immediately following Operation Storm, as far as I can recall, there were no other military commands in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Other than who?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Other than General Cermak and two individuals with him, and me and my liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, that's the sum total of the people that you noticed in the military in Knin after, or in terms of the command, was General Cermak, two other people, and you and your liaison officers, after Operation Storm finished?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We're talking about the first couple of days. I can't be absolutely precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Getting back to the bit about Mr. Plestina. I didn't notice that in either of your statements about the visit from your superior, Plestina. Any reason why you didn't mention that and him coming down and giving you this -- this order, or whatever the talk was about where to report to or whether to inform people about crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no new orders on informing and reporting crimes, not in that sense. I was never given any such orders. When my superior was with me, then there was no need for me to report on his coming to visit me. So we discussed the situation, as it was, what it was that we had to do in the future, and we were talking about the need to redefine the role of the UN members after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just getting back to -- when we you were talking about once you heard the news item and you said that you if you became aware of crimes who would you inform. What if you saw HV members committing a crime, or one of your CALO officers saw a HV member committing a crime, that's the same thing, you just tell the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would inform the civilian police, and we would also include this in our daily report that was sent to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, you said before that -- in terms of the Military Command in Knin after Operation Storm, you said it was General Cermak and a few other people. I'm wondering if, given your position, if you can explain, or if can you make sense of why General Cermak would tell Prosecution investigators that after Operation Storm, General Gotovina would come and go, that he left for Bosnia but he would come back, and that General Gotovina remained the commander of the Split Military District all the time, and that he was in charge of the military in the area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: What I knew about General Gotovina's duties at the time - in other words, up until the 5th of August, 1995 - and on that last day I was with General Gotovina, he was, at the time, the commander of the Split Military District. From that moment on, a lot -- a long time passed before I saw General Gotovina again, and I know, in the mean time based on the report of my deputy, I know that there was a celebration of some sort in the Knin fortress where General Gotovina was present and I think also General Forand. I was not in Knin on that day. I was in the field because I had other assignments in other areas. I only heard about, this, and I heard that General Gotovina was in Knin. But I did not see him on that day or in the days following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, are you aware that General Forand, at his first meeting with General Gotovina, which was on the 8th of August, 1995, in Knin, that when he met with him he complained to General Gotovina about the lack of discipline of HV troops and that they were looting and burning the town, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, that is not an accurate depiction of the record. I would ask to point in the record where General Forand says that was the subject of discussion with General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I will try to assist, Mr. President. I will read from P333, paragraph 7, on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, so that I have an opportunity to find that. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'll read it to you, Mr. Lukovic. General Forand explains that the first meeting that he with General Gotovina, he says: "... which was the first meeting I had with him after Operation Storm. After reviewing the UNCRO situation reports for that period, I now recall that this meeting actually took place on 8 August 1995, although it is not reflected in the sitrep for that date. I do recall complaining to General Gotovina about the lack of discipline of his troops and that they were looting and burning in the town. General Gotovina referred to -- referred me to General Cermak for these and any other complaints." That was the end of the quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just -- this is a contextual issue regarding General Forand. It is put in context to some degree by the Prosecutor in the fact that there was nothing in the UN sitrep talking about this and that it was then a subject of discussion on cross-examination, and I can go back and ferret it out concerning General Forand. But -- suffice it to say, that, at this particular point it would be helpful if we take a look to see exactly what was put in the sitrep, because there is no discussion about this. And I don't expect to go back in and re-track everything that's in the transcript, Judge. I know the difficulties inherent in that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, your objection was that this is not an accurate depiction of the record. I would ask that we be directed to where General Forand says that. Now, the wording chosen by Mr. Carrier are literally the same as the ones we find in the statement of General Forand. And now to come up with issues like, It is not reflected in the sitrep, Mr. Carrier did not say that. In all written reports and statements we find this; he said - and that was his question - that whether the witness was aware that such complaint by General Gotovina were expressed during this visit. What Mr. Carrier said accurately depicts, at least, the statement given by General Forand. And I would have to check whether anywhere General Forand, during cross-examination, said that this was not what he complained about. If you have a clear reference for me, please give it then I'll check it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as an officer of the Court, I do not, at this particular juncture -- I will take a look through that as to how we discussed this particular matter, and I will refresh myself with my colleagues on this bantering -- the discussion back and fourth with General Forand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Without this actual knowledge, at least, your objection, which was limited to that it does not accurately depict the record, it certainly depicts the statement of General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In isolation, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, yes -- Mr. Kehoe. Let's give Mr. Carrier an opportunity to proceed. You may proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The part that I just read to you about what General Forand said, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this particular instances, because I think this is -- this relates to the day that I mentioned earlier, when both General Gotovina and General Forand were at this celebration, this event, at the Knin fortress. And I think I was -- I was not there on that day, but I can conjecture that my deputy might have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, is it fair to say - you just mentioned that you weren't there that day - but is it fair to say that you don't know the full extent of Mr. Cermak's contacts with internationals, meaning the contact that he with them, nor are you fully aware of what General Cermak did with the information that he received from the internationals with whom he had contact?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of these contacts or almost most of these contacts, I received the information on, even if I was not present on that particular day. And because my area of responsibility had to do with the liaising, as a liaison officer for three different areas, three Military Districts, Lika, Sector South, and Split Military District all the way to Dubrovnik, which means that there were occasions where I had to be in those areas on assignments. But I was advised and informed of most of what had happened in the meantime, either by my deputy or by one of the liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, were you aware that General Cermak had given his phone number to some internationals and that some of those internationals used it to call General Cermak on occasion in order to try to have restrictions on their movement lifted?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a phone line in General Cermak's office which most of us -- or all of us used, for the most part, including myself, and I'm referring to the time when that phone line was first set up. So UN representatives, either those from the command of the former Sector South or the military observers or whatever their roles were, whenever they called or kept in touch over the phone, they would use that phone, the phone that was in the office of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: My question was whether or not you were aware that he gave out his number and that that number was used.

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I answered your question. They knew -- they had this phone number because we used this phone number in our daily communications with UN representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So that's a yes, you knew that General Cermak gave out his phone number; and, yes, you knew that internationals called that phone number to contact General Cermak in order to have restrictions lifted on their movement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any instance where they called him directly because the contacts and meetings with General Cermak were arranged through my office, and it is quite certain that most of the time they were arranged by way of this telephone line. But whether General Cermak provided this phone number to them or me, I really couldn't tell you with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukovic, you said before that you were away at times, and that you're confident, I take it, that either your CALOs or your deputy or somebody would be informing you about what they were doing in the context that General Cermak was having. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukovic, in your 2004 statement, you told Prosecution investigators that you had no knowledge about the killings in Grubori, other than what you had heard on the media and that you were unaware of any of your liaison officers going to Grubori or submitting a report about it. Now --

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukovic, given this statement, I take it that you would have no explanation as to why one of your CALOs would be involved in visiting that village during the relevant period, seeing dead bodies, and reporting in writing to General Cermak on that issue, would you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, but I'm not certain of this. Because of the time that has elapsed, I can't really recall whether General Cermak or the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, just in terms of General Cermak's contact with the internationals, General Cermak has given a statement to the Prosecution investigators in which he indicated that there was a liaison officer from an international organisation stationed in his HQ who was given his own space and had free access in the building and was with them all the time in the building. And I'm wondering if you can reconcile your statement, where you say, in your 2009 statement, that the UN officer assigned to General Cermak's office sat in your office. He remained there a few days before returning to the UN barracks. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that the person is the same. It was for a very short period of time because they were trying to find a way for us to communicate with UN representatives as efficiently as possible and provide for the fastest possible way of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So other than it being the same person, you can't account for the other discrepancies between what General Cermak told Prosecution investigators and what you put in your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I don't see anything else. I believe that we're talking about the same person here. And that functioned, for a while, for a short time. And then the UN decided to withdraw that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, are you aware that -- sorry, I'll start again. Mr. Lukovic, you state that you were not aware of any communication between General Gotovina and General Cermak, and correct me if I'm wrong on this point, but I'm presuming that you meant after August 6th, and that you also said that you doubted if there was any such communication between them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The first part, when you asked me whether I knew or I didn't know about the -- that meeting, after such a long time I can't really remember. As for the second part of your question, where you mention communication, what do you mean? I didn't quite understand that part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'll read your words, which is on page 8 of your 2004 statement to the Prosecution, at paragraph 48, part way down, where you say -- sorry, maybe I should put it a little bit in context for you. At the beginning of paragraph you say: "I did not have any contact with General Gotovina after the meeting in Knin on the 6th of August." And unless my friends across the way want me to add anything else, I will move down to another part where you say: "I am not aware of any communication between General Cermak and General Gotovina and personally I doubt if there was." So I was asking about your words and asking if you could -- if that's correct. And adding to that, if can you explain the basis for your opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if I understood the proceedings here correctly, then I believe that the corrections of my statement have been admitted into evidence. I remember the part that you just mentioned very well, but I also remember that the translation was very ambiguous, that it was never unambiguous. As I was reading the Croatian part of my statement, in that part it can be understood in any way you want. And that's when you're talking about that statement. Now, as to whether General Cermak and General Gotovina communicated, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So I take it then you wouldn't have been aware that General Cermak told the Prosecution investigators that General Gotovina was informed of everything that was written to him from the internationals. Would you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, actually? I simply don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, can you explain who ordered all of your original reports in Zadar to be burned in 1999 and why exactly that was done?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. When an order came for the office to be closed down -- or, rather, the Department of that office that was my former department for Sector South, then an order also came from Zagreb from the superior office, and I believe that the person was no longer Brigadier Plestina. I believe that he was already retired. But it's neither here nor there. It could have been his deputy who then became the head of that department. His name was Brigadier Kukec. That procedure is more or less normal in any such situation. An office is being closed down, and it had been made sure that all the reports from my department were in the archives of the Ministry of the Defence in Zagreb and then the copy that was archived in Zadar could be burned under the supervision of a commission consisting of three men. All the documents were filed and the report of the procedure was sent to Zagreb. But, I repeat, before that, we had received official information that all the copies of our reports had already been archived in the Ministry of Defence in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, was it the copies that were burned, or was it the originals that were burned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: All sorts of documents, originals and copies alike. If you don't understand my answer, I can illustrate my answer with an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, it's okay, I understand. Copies and originals were burned. Now, just a moment ago you were talking about ambiguous translations. And, Mr. Lukovic, I want to draw your attention to some specific examples of changes and explanations that you've provided for just two of the paragraphs in your original 2004 statement, and then I want to ask you some questions about that. Now, specifically at paragraph 27 on page 5 in the English of your 2004 statement, wherein, correct me if I'm wrong, but you're describing a walk and observations -- sorry. You're talking about some observations that you made on 5th and 6th of August in Knin in 1995. And your original statement reads: "There were many Croatian soldiers in the town and there was much euphoria and some of the soldiers were shooting in the air." Which you have now changed to: "There was a very small number of Croatian soldiers in the town." And in the same paragraph, you said that you were woken up on the 6th of August by shooting and you saw "a Croatian soldier shooting at a dog." Which now you want to add the words to make that dog "pretty rabid." And at paragraph 31 of your 2004 statement, which is on page 6 in the English and 6 in the B/C/S, you originally describe walking in Knin with Mr. Dondo on 6th of August, 1995, and you report seeing, among other things, signs of destruction and looting by Croatian soldiers. You report observing patrols by ordinary soldiers, some military individuals behaving badly. However, you want this changed, or you've change this to -- to -- so that it reads that the patrols were exclusively conducted by the military police, and that there were no -- sorry. Quote: "There were no signs of destruction in the town." And that: "There was a very small number of Croatian soldiers in the town of Knin and they were not behaving badly." Now, Mr. Lukovic, given your most recent version which indicates that, basically, right after Operation Storm, you observed no signs of destruction in Knin and very few HV members who were not behaving badly in Knin, and I'm not sure if you're suggesting that they were also cleaning the town of rabid dogs. But can I ask to you explain these changes in light of a few things. At paragraph 29, which is on page 6 of your 2004 statement, you talk about a 6 of August meeting in the Knin fortress and you describe General Gotovina was very angry at what he had seen when he arrived in Knin and at the misbehaviour of some Croatian soldiers and that he had accused the commanders of lack of control over their men which was shameful to the Croatian Army. Can you explain how you understood that at the time, the anger, and what you understood General Gotovina to be angry at, given your description of Knin as it is in your 2009 statement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will gladly explain that. In light of the fact how you represented things, even a perfunctory look would reveal a lot of contradictions, three or for at least. First of all, I arrived in Knin on the 5th of August by helicopter. I arrived with five or six other officers. We landed at the football pitch, and, on the southern part, we made our way into Knin. I am emphasizing the southern part, because, according to everything I know, and in view of the number of soldiers that I saw as I was entering Knin from the centre of Knin towards the northern part of Knin, I saw a few groups of soldiers who were rejoicing, celebrating, and shooting in the air wanting to show their joy at Knin being ours. So when I'm talking about people shooting in the air, I'm talking about the first day when the Croatian Army entered Knin. And I'm not talking about the southern part of Knin, but, rather, about its northern part. When you say that I saw traces of destruction in Knin, I don't know whether we're -- this is due to bad interpretation, and I apologise to my colleagues, the interpreters. I would like to point out at the moment, and I've already written it down several times, as I was passing through Knin -- to be very precise, I saw the places where three grenades fell and I can repeat. One was on the wall of the so-called JNA home, the house that -- that housed my office and Mr. Cermak's office. The second was on a civilian house across the road. And the third shell trace was on the football pitch where we landed with the helicopter. On the following day, when we were woken up by the shots, those shots were fired by that soldier who had shot at a dog. We went out, and there were no other soldiers there.
